nameStory: The "creeping" part of this buttercup's name comes from its sneaky habit of spreading across the ground with runners, like strawberry plants do. The "buttercup" name comes from an old folk belief that cows eating these golden flowers would produce richer, more golden butter - though in reality, cattle usually avoid these plants because they taste quite bitter!
description: Creeping buttercup is a low-growing perennial wildflower that spreads by sending out runners along the ground, forming patches in lawns and moist areas. It produces bright yellow, five-petaled flowers that look like they've been polished with butter, sitting atop stems about 6-18 inches tall. The plant has distinctive three-part leaves that are often marked with pale spots or patterns, and it can quickly colonize an area through its creeping stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with five glossy, waxy-looking petals that reflect light like tiny mirrors. Each flower is about 3/4 inch across with a cluster of yellow stamens in the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves divided into segments, often with pale silvery or whitish blotches that look like water stains. The leaves feel somewhat thick and waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Spreads by long runners (stolons) that creep along the ground and root at nodes, much like strawberry plants. Forms expanding patches rather than staying in one clump.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flowering stems are upright and slightly hairy, while the creeping runners lie flat on the ground and are smooth. The runners can be several feet long.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: All parts of the plant have a slightly waxy, thick feel and bitter taste. The sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, leaving a slight burning sensation.

habitat: Thrives in moist, rich soils in lawns, gardens, meadows, and along stream banks throughout New England. Particularly common in areas with poor drainage or compacted soil where grass struggles to grow. Often found mixed with dandelions and clover in disturbed areas from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and flowers begin blooming in late spring, with the distinctive pale leaf markings most visible on fresh growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers appearing continuously. Runners actively spread and root at this time, creating new plants.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in favorable conditions. Leaves remain green and the plant continues to spread via runners.
seasonality.winter: In milder areas, leaves may persist through winter as a low rosette. Runners and established root systems survive to regrow in spring.

funFact: Creeping buttercup is such an aggressive spreader that a single plant can colonize an area the size of a small room in just one growing season, sending out runners up to 3 feet long that root at every node like a natural cloning machine!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other buttercups, but remember the "three C's": Creeping buttercup has **C**reeping runners, **C**hunk-shaped (three-part) leaves with pale markings, and grows in **C**ompacted or moist soils. Meadow buttercup grows in tall clumps without runners, while bulbous buttercup has a swollen stem base.
contextualKnowledge: This European native has become naturalized across New England and is often considered a lawn weed due to its aggressive spreading habit. The plant contains compounds that can cause blistering if handled extensively, which is why it's sometimes called "sitfast" - referring to the sores it could cause.
compareHints: Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground. Its three-part leaves with pale markings are also more distinctive than the deeply divided, fernlike leaves of most other buttercups in our area.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
